title: The Stall in Swift Hall: Iasi, Perugia, Groningen, and the Historian of Ecstasy

segments.name: The House on Strada Sfantul Atanasie

stops.name: Iasi, birth in the Bogdan house
stops.date_confidence: Birth date and city attested (English Wikipedia; the FBI investigative file gives the same date and birthplace independently). The street address, 13 Strada Sfantul Atanasie, is confirmed as the Bogdan and Culianu family house by the Iasi property investigation in 7iasi.ro, which also gives the 1801 build date and the Sararie location; coordinates are the Nominatim geocode of the street, 47.1702 / 27.5858, correcting an earlier figure that fell 775 m south. The 1926 Bogdan acquisition is family chronology, not independently located.
stops.campa: A son is born to Elena Culianu, born Bogdan, professor of inorganic chemistry at the university, and to Sergiu-Andrei Culianu, trained in mathematics and physics in Paris and in law at Iasi. The house on the Sararie slope was built around 1801 and came to the Bogdan family between the wars: a house of laboratories and law books, where God is not a subject at table. He is the second child. His sister Tereza, born in October 1945, is four years old the winter he is carried in.
suggested_refs: The Bogdan-Culianu house at 13 Strada Sfantul Atanasie, Iasi, built c. 1801, restored 2004-2010
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu'
FBI investigative file, 'Ioan Culianu Part 01 of 01' (archive.org OCR text)
7iasi.ro, investigative article on the Culianu house

stops.name: Manastirea Varatec, the prayer of the heart
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The episode rests entirely on Tereza Culianu-Petrescu's chronology 'O biografie' in the memorial volume edited by Sorin Antohi; no independent source was reached. Date is an ordering device inside the stated 1950s-1960s span, not a recorded year. Coordinates are the Nominatim geocode of Manastirea Varatec, Agapia, Neamt, 47.1398 / 26.2683, correcting an earlier figure 18 km west in open country.
stops.campa: The family takes its summers in the Neamt hills near the monastery of Varatec, where the nuns keep the offices in a valley of walnut and orchard. Manea, once a nun and now the household's nanny, teaches the children the prayer of the heart: the Jesus prayer said on the breath until the breath says it without them. The parents are scientists and unbelievers, and the one working technique of ecstasy in the household comes in through the servant. Whether the boy keeps saying it, and for how long, nobody records.
suggested_refs: Tereza Culianu-Petrescu, 'O biografie', in Sorin Antohi (ed.), Ioan Petru Culianu: Omul si opera
sources: Tereza Culianu-Petrescu, family chronology, in Antohi (ed.), Omul si opera (archive.org)

stops.name: Iasi, the father dies and the son takes philology
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, from the family chronology; the year of the father's death is given as 1964, when Culianu was fourteen. Contradiction flagged and not resolved: the FBI file records Sergiu-Andrei Culianu's birth as 1903, the family chronology as 1904. The mother's chair in inorganic chemistry at Alexandru Ioan Cuza University and her 1907 birth year are attested in the FBI file. The 1967 secondary-school ranking is tradition only. Pinned at the family house.
stops.campa: Sergiu-Andrei Culianu dies when his son is fourteen, and the household contracts to a mother, a sister, and a boy. Elena keeps her chair in inorganic chemistry; the family keeps the house on the Sararie slope. Ioan finishes secondary school at the head of a science track, which is the expected road for a professor's son in a state that funds physics and watches philology. He chooses philology. On every application form in the country there is a box for the father's occupation, and the box now reads deceased, which in 1964 is a kind of protection.
suggested_refs: Alexandru Ioan Cuza University, Iasi, where Elena Culianu held the chair in inorganic chemistry
sources: FBI investigative file, 'Ioan Culianu Part 01 of 01' (archive.org OCR text)
Tereza Culianu-Petrescu, family chronology, in Antohi (ed.), Omul si opera

stops.name: University of Bucharest, the transfer to Italian
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the sequence, attested as to the outcome. English Wikipedia gives the enrolment in 1967 and the transfer after a year from Romanian literature to the Italian section of the Faculty of Romance, Classical, and Oriental Languages; the month is an ordering default. The eastern languages studied alongside are reported in the biographical tradition and in the interlock survey, not in a document reached.
stops.campa: He enters the University of Bucharest in Romanian literature and moves after a year into the Italian section of the Faculty of Romance, Classical, and Oriental Languages. Italian is a door. It opens onto the Renaissance, onto Ficino and Bruno and the whole magical bibliography of the sixteenth century, a shelf the regime has not thought to police as closely as it polices the moderns. Alongside the Italian he works at Sanskrit, Hindi, Arabic and Hebrew. He is eighteen years old.
suggested_refs: The Faculty of Romance, Classical, and Oriental Languages, University of Bucharest
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu'
University of Chicago Library, finding aid for the Ioan P. Culianu Papers

stops.name: Grozavesti, the candlelit procession
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and weakly supported. The episode comes from the family and biographical tradition; the research pass located no arrest file and no independent record of it. Coordinates are the Nominatim geocode of the Grozavesti district, Sector 6, 44.4427 / 26.0604, correcting an earlier figure 675 m west. Day within December not recorded.
stops.campa: On a December night students carry candles from the university out to the dormitories at Grozavesti, singing carols, which in 1968 is not a devotional act but an unauthorised assembly with open flame. Culianu is stopped with his girlfriend and questioned. No arrest file has been found for the episode; it survives only in what the family remembered afterward and told later. Somewhere in these years the Securitate opens a file on him. Whether this night is what opened it, nobody can now say.
suggested_refs: The Grozavesti student dormitory complex, Bucharest
sources: Family and biographical tradition, per the research dossier (no arrest file located)

stops.name: Bucharest, the party card
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the subject himself, in a hostile forum. The membership and the reason are stated in Culianu's sworn December 1989 affidavit to the United States immigration service, reproduced in the FBI investigative file; the affidavit is a primary record and the quotation below is verbatim from it. Month given as January 1970 in the biographical record; day is an ordering default. The 1973 expulsion in absentia is reported in the same account.
stops.campa: In January he takes a Romanian Communist Party card. He is twenty, four semesters from a degree, with a Securitate file thicker than his thesis notes and a dead father in the box on the form. The card buys quiet. It does not buy a passport, and it does not close the file. He holds it two and a half years, until Bucharest expels him in absentia for not coming home from Italy. Nineteen years later, under oath to the American immigration service of a country that holds such memberships against the men who took them, he explains it in a single sentence.
stops.quote: My circumstances at the time forced me to become a member, although I have never embraced any communist ideology.
stops.quote_source: Ioan Culianu, sworn affidavit to the United States Immigration and Naturalization Service, December 1989, reproduced in the FBI investigative file
suggested_refs: Culianu's December 1989 INS affidavit, reproduced in the FBI investigative file
sources: FBI investigative file, 'Ioan Culianu Part 01 of 01' (archive.org OCR text)

stops.name: University of Bucharest, Ficino and the letters to Chicago
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the degree, contradictory as to the month. English Wikipedia gives graduation in Italian language and literature in 1972; the chronology lens dates it May 1972 and the geography lens June 1972, and the contradiction is left standing. The thesis on Marsilio Ficino and Renaissance Platonism, supervised by Nina Facon, and the reported 9.87 average come from Culianu's own curriculum vitae and affidavit as cited in the dossier, not from a document refetched here. The 1971 papers sent to Eliade are family tradition.
stops.campa: He graduates in Italian language and literature with a thesis on Marsilio Ficino and Platonism in the Renaissance, directed by Nina Facon. The year before, he had posted to Chicago two papers of his own, one on coincidentia oppositorum in Giordano Bruno, one on sun and moon symbolism, addressed to Mircea Eliade: a Romanian who had left and become the most famous historian of religions alive. Eliade answers. They write to each other in Romanian for the next nineteen years, and for the first three of them they never meet.
suggested_refs: 'Marsilio Ficino e il platonismo nel Rinascimento', graduation thesis, University of Bucharest, 1972
The Eliade-Culianu correspondence, published as Dialoguri intrerupte (Polirom, 2004; reissued 2013)
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu'
Tereza Culianu-Petrescu, family chronology, in Antohi (ed.), Omul si opera

stops.name: Perugia, Piazza Fortebraccio
stops.date_confidence: Attested. English Wikipedia confirms Perugia and the grant of political asylum in Italy in July 1972; the date of departure is given by Culianu himself in the December 1989 affidavit reproduced in the FBI file, quoted below verbatim. The family chronology gives the same 4 July date independently.
stops.campa: Two weeks after the graduation he leaves Bucharest on a one-month Italian government scholarship to the University for Foreigners at Perugia, a grant that entitles a student to summer courses in Piazza Fortebraccio and obliges him to come home at the end of them. He arrives on the fourth of July. He does not come home. Behind him are his mother, his sister, the house on the Sararie slope and a party card he no longer needs. Ahead of him are thirty days of lawful residence and after that nothing at all.
stops.quote: I defected from Romania on July 4, 1972, never again to return there.
stops.quote_source: Ioan Culianu, sworn affidavit to the United States Immigration and Naturalization Service, December 1989, reproduced in the FBI investigative file
suggested_refs: Universita per Stranieri di Perugia, Piazza Fortebraccio
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu'
FBI investigative file, 'Ioan Culianu Part 01 of 01' (archive.org OCR text)

stops.name: Padriciano, the camp on the karst
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the site is an inference. That Culianu spent roughly five months in Italian refugee facilities before the December 1972 recognition is in the biographical record; that the Trieste facility was Padriciano is the researcher's own inference from what the standard Trieste reception centre of the period was, and is not confirmed by any source reached. Coordinates are the Nominatim geocode of Padriciano, 45.6581 / 13.8397, correcting an earlier figure 4.3 km south near Basovizza.
stops.campa: The scholarship lapses and the student becomes a case number. On the karst above Trieste the Italian state parks the eastern Europeans who go out and do not go back: barracks, a canteen, a queue, a wait measured in months. He has a Bucharest degree in Italian, a thesis on Ficino and no papers. No source reached names which of the Trieste facilities held him. The five months inside the Italian reception system are in the record; the address is not.
suggested_refs: The Padriciano refugee reception centre above Trieste, standard facility for eastern European arrivals in the 1970s
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu' (asylum, July 1972)
Family and biographical tradition, per the research dossier

stops.name: Latina, the wrists
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The suicide attempt rests on family testimony and on Ted Anton's interviews as characterised in the secondary biographical literature; it was not verified against Anton's book directly in this pass, and the sources do not agree whether it happened at Trieste or at Latina. The recognition as a Convention refugee on 13 December 1972 is from the family chronology; the general fact of Italian asylum in 1972 is attested by English Wikipedia.
stops.campa: At Latina, south of Rome, in the largest of the Italian refugee centres, Culianu cuts his wrists. The wounds clot. He is found, and he lives. He is twenty-two years old, five months out of a country he cannot re-enter and not yet admitted to any other. On the thirteenth of December Italy recognises him as a Convention refugee and the case number becomes a person again. He does not write about the wrists afterward. The sources do not agree whether it happened here or at Trieste.
suggested_refs: Ted Anton, Eros, Magic, and the Murder of Professor Culianu (Northwestern University Press, 1996)
sources: Family testimony and Ted Anton's interviews, per the research dossier
English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu'

stops.name: Via Appia Antica, the weeks in the community
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the site is approximate. The episode is family and biographical tradition; no source reached names the house or the order, and the coordinates stand for the Via Appia Antica corridor generally rather than a located community. Date is an ordering device inside the reported 1972-1973 span.
stops.campa: For some weeks he tries a religious community out along the Via Appia Antica, on the road of tombs south of Rome, and then leaves it. No source reached names the house, the order, the reason for going in or the reason for coming out. He is twenty-three. The ecstatic techniques, the soul said to leave the body: all of it is already his subject, and for some weeks he is inside a house that practises it. Then he is outside again, applying for another scholarship.
suggested_refs: The Via Appia Antica corridor south of Rome and its religious communities
sources: Family and biographical tradition, per the research dossier

stops.name: Domus Nostra, Milan
stops.date_confidence: Institution attested, residence reconstructed. English Wikipedia confirms the affiliation with the Universita Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Milan and the November 1975 doctorate; the Domus Nostra residence, the material hardship, and Ugo Bianchi's mentorship are from the family chronology. The Antonio Lupatelli Prize at Perugia in March 1973 and the expulsion in absentia from the Romanian Communist Party the same year are both reported in the biographical record and not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: In March he had finished the Corsi di Alta Cultura at Perugia at the top of the list and taken the Antonio Lupatelli Prize; in Bucharest, that same year, the party expels him in absentia from a membership he had held for two and a half years. In October he moves into Domus Nostra, a residence attached to the Catholic University of Milan. Ugo Bianchi, historian of religions and student of dualism, takes him on and sets him to Gnosticism. He is poor that winter, and the library at Largo Gemelli is across the courtyard.
suggested_refs: The library of the Universita Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Largo Gemelli, Milan
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu'
Tereza Culianu-Petrescu, family chronology, in Antohi (ed.), Omul si opera

stops.name: Paris, meeting Eliade
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the meeting, attested as to the relation. The first face-to-face meeting in September 1974 and the inscribed book come from the family chronology; no venue is documented and the coordinates are the canonical Paris pin used across the atlas rather than a located address. The mentorship itself is independently confirmed by the University of Chicago Library finding aid, which describes Culianu as mentored by Mircea Eliade.
stops.campa: After three years of letters the two men meet in person, in Paris. The older man is sixty-seven, holds the chair at Chicago and has behind him a Bucharest of the 1930s he does not discuss. The younger is twenty-four, stateless, living on a residence permit and a reader's card. Eliade calls him the best of the coming generation. No source reached names the venue or the hour or who else was in the room; what the family chronology keeps is that Eliade inscribed a book to him, and that Culianu kept it.
suggested_refs: The Eliade-Culianu correspondence, 1971-1986, published as Dialoguri intrerupte
sources: Tereza Culianu-Petrescu, family chronology, in Antohi (ed.), Omul si opera
University of Chicago Library, finding aid for the Ioan P. Culianu Papers

stops.name: Swift Hall, the first Chicago semester
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The 1975 postdoctoral semester with Eliade and Carsten Colpe, the New York and New England travel, and the meeting with Hans Jonas are all from the family chronology; the University of Chicago finding aid documents his later Chicago career but says nothing about a 1975 visiting semester, so an earlier attested tag here was unearned and is withdrawn. Month is an ordering default. Coordinates are the Nominatim geocode of Swift Hall, 1025 East 58th Street, 41.7889 / -87.6001, correcting an earlier figure 340 m east near Woodlawn Avenue.
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic for a semester at the Divinity School, working beside Eliade and the Berlin historian Carsten Colpe in the building where, sixteen years on, he will be shot. He travels to New York and through New England and meets Hans Jonas, whose Gnosis und spatantiker Geist is the book his own doctorate is being written against. Jonas reads the second-century Gnostics through Heidegger and existential philosophy. Culianu is twenty-five and halfway through a thesis arguing that the anxiety Jonas found in the second century belongs to his own.
suggested_refs: Hans Jonas, Gnosis und spatantiker Geist (1934-1954)
Swift Hall, University of Chicago Divinity School, 1025 East 58th Street
sources: Tereza Culianu-Petrescu, family chronology, in Antohi (ed.), Omul si opera
University of Chicago Library, finding aid for the Ioan P. Culianu Papers

stops.name: Universita Cattolica, the doctorate on Hans Jonas
stops.date_confidence: Attested. English Wikipedia gives the doctorate in history of religions at the Universita Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Milan, November 1975. Thesis title varies by source and the variance is left standing: Wikipedia gives 'Gnosticismo e pensiero contemporaneo: Hans Jonas', while the book published from it by L'Erma di Bretschneider in 1985 is titled 'Gnosticismo e pensiero moderno: Hans Jonas' per OpenLibrary. Day is an ordering default.
stops.campa: He takes the Italian dottore in lettere in the history of religions at the Catholic University with a thesis on Hans Jonas and Gnosticism, supervised by Bianchi. The argument is that Jonas found in the second century the anxiety of his own century, and that the finding tells us more about the twentieth than about the second. Ideas are to be handled as objects with a structure of their own; the interpreter's mood is evidence about the interpreter. He is twenty-five. It is the first of his three doctorates.
suggested_refs: Gnosticismo e pensiero moderno: Hans Jonas (L'Erma di Bretschneider, 1985), the thesis revised into a book
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu'
OpenLibrary record for Gnosticismo e pensiero moderno: Hans Jonas

segments.name: Groningen, the Decade in the North

stops.name: Groningen, Broerstraat 5
stops.date_confidence: Year attested, month and sponsor reconstructed. English Wikipedia gives the University of Groningen appointment and the span 1976-1985, teaching the history of Romanian culture. The specific November start and Willem Noomen's sponsorship are from the family chronology and are not in the cited source; they are carried here as reconstruction.
stops.campa: The Netherlands gives him what Italy did not, which is a salary. He joins the University of Groningen as an assistant in Romanian language and culture, on the support of the Romance scholar Willem Noomen, and he will hold the post for ten years. The teaching is Romanian culture to Dutch undergraduates in a northern city with a great university and almost no Romanians in it. The research is everything else. From the office at Broerstraat 5 he publishes in four languages and applies, year on year, for the chairs that do not come.
suggested_refs: The Academiegebouw, Broerstraat 5, University of Groningen
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu'
Tereza Culianu-Petrescu, family chronology, in Antohi (ed.), Omul si opera

stops.name: Groningen, the book on Eliade
stops.date_confidence: Publication attested in the bibliographic record cited across the biographical sources; the 1978 date is consistent with the Groningen output described by English Wikipedia, though no publisher record was refetched in this pass. Month and day are ordering defaults. The Popperian reading of the book is the standard characterisation in the secondary literature and is carried as such.
stops.campa: He publishes Mircea Eliade, the first monograph on his own master, in Italian, with the publisher Cittadella. It is written from inside the discipleship and it is not a homage. Culianu puts Karl Popper's test of falsifiability to Eliade's phenomenology of the sacred and reports where the phenomenology fails it: an archetype that cannot be refuted cannot be confirmed either. He is twenty-eight and has been writing to the man for seven years. Eliade reads the book. The correspondence continues without a break.
suggested_refs: Ioan Petru Culianu, Mircea Eliade (Cittadella, 1978)
sources: Publication record cited across the biographical literature
English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu'

stops.name: Groningen, Carmen Georgescu
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Both dates, the meeting on 19 July 1979 and the civil marriage on 28 December 1979, come from Tereza Culianu-Petrescu's chronology and family correspondence; neither was independently confirmed. English Wikipedia independently records only that he was divorced from a first wife by the time of his death. The pin is the Groningen university pin, not a located address.
stops.campa: He meets Carmen-Zoe Georgescu, Romanian-born and long resident in the Netherlands, in July, and marries her in December of the same year. Her son Andrei becomes his stepson. For the first time since Perugia he has an address that is a home rather than an allocation, in a country that has given him documents and a wage and a decade of work. The chronology his sister keeps records a civil ceremony in the Netherlands and, the following year, a wedding party on the Seine: two dates for one marriage. It lasts, on paper, seven years.
suggested_refs: Tereza Culianu-Petrescu's chronology and the family correspondence on the two ceremonies
sources: Tereza Culianu-Petrescu, family chronology, in Antohi (ed.), Omul si opera
English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu'

stops.name: The Normandie on the Seine
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the location is approximate. The celebration aboard the boat Normandie is reported in the family correspondence as characterised in the dossier; no month is recorded, so the date defaults to January as an ordering device, and the coordinates are a central-Seine point rather than a documented mooring.
stops.campa: The wedding celebration is held aboard the Normandie, a boat on the Seine, in the city where he met Eliade six years earlier and where he will take two doctorates. Romanian Paris is thick that year with people who left exactly as he left, on a scholarship or a visa or a conference, and did not go back. The photographs pass into the family correspondence, which is the only reason anyone knows the boat had a name. Nobody wrote down the mooring, or the month.
suggested_refs: Family correspondence describing the 1980 celebration aboard the Normandie
sources: Family correspondence, per the research dossier

stops.name: Sorbonne, 47 rue des Ecoles
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The thesis title, the 17 June 1980 date and Michel Meslin's direction are from the academic record as characterised in the secondary literature; independent verification was attempted through theses.fr and data.idref.fr and both refused connections from this network. An earlier attested tag on this event conflicted with the same event tagged as reconstruction elsewhere in the research pool, and the weaker tag is kept. Coordinates for 47 rue des Ecoles are sound.
stops.campa: He defends a doctorat de troisieme cycle in the history and philosophy of religions under Michel Meslin: Experiences de l'extase et symboles de l'ascension, de l'hellenisme au Moyen Age. The subject is the soul's journey out of the body, catalogued across a thousand years of Mediterranean religion, from the Hellenistic ascent texts to the medieval visions of the other world. Parts of it will become Psychanodia and Experiences de l'extase. He is thirty, holds two doctorates from two countries, and has a permanent post in neither.
suggested_refs: Psychanodia I (1983) and Experiences de l'extase (Payot, 1984), drawn from this thesis
sources: Academic record as characterised in the secondary biographical literature
theses.fr and data.idref.fr, attempted and unreachable (connection refused)

stops.name: Groningen, Eros et magie a la Renaissance
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the work, reconstructed as to the pin. The University of Chicago Press page for the 1987 English translation confirms the French original and its argument; the 1984 French publication year is from the bibliographic record. The chronology lens places the publication at Paris, but Culianu was living and working at Groningen, so the stop sits where the writing happened rather than where the imprint was. Month and day are ordering defaults.
stops.campa: From the Groningen office he finishes Eros et magie a la Renaissance. 1484. Frances Yates had opened this ground twenty years earlier at the Warburg; Culianu goes over it again and comes out with a harder claim. Ficino's magic is a discipline of the imagination. Bruno's is a technique of erotic manipulation practised on crowds, and its direct descendant is the modern operator of publicity, whose instrument is a phantasm raised inside the receiver's own mind. Flammarion publishes it in Paris in 1984.
suggested_refs: Frances Yates, Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (Warburg Institute, 1964)
Eros and Magic in the Renaissance, trans. Margaret Cook, foreword by Mircea Eliade (University of Chicago Press, 1987)
sources: University of Chicago Press, book page for Eros and Magic in the Renaissance

segments.name: Chicago, the Death of the Master

stops.name: Swift Hall, the return to Chicago
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the date is contested. The University of Chicago finding aid says only that he was visiting lecturer and then professor in the Divinity School, with no dates; English Wikipedia gives 'University of Chicago (1988-1991): professor of history of religions', not a March 1986 return; the family chronology gives the earlier visiting appointment. The 'Hiram Thomas Guest Lecturer' title appears in nothing reached. Both readings are left standing. Coordinates as corrected for Swift Hall.
stops.campa: He comes back to the Divinity School, first as a visitor and then as professor of the history of religions, into the building where he had sat as a postdoctoral guest eleven years earlier. Chicago is Eliade's city; the chair is in Eliade's field; everyone in Swift Hall understands what the arrangement means. He is thirty-six, holds two doctorates, is finishing a third, and has been applying for permanent posts since he was twenty-six. When exactly the appointment began is not agreed between the sources.
suggested_refs: Swift Hall, University of Chicago Divinity School
sources: University of Chicago Library, finding aid for the Ioan P. Culianu Papers
English Wikipedia, 'Ioan Petru Culianu'
Tereza Culianu-Petrescu, family chronology, in Antohi (ed.), Omul si opera

stops.name: Bernard Mitchell Hospital, the last eight days
stops.date_confidence: Eliade's hospitalisation and death on 22 April 1986 are attested and carry their own stop in the atlas file for Eliade, which pins them at these coordinates; the pin is inherited unchanged. Culianu's presence at the bedside is from the family chronology and Ted Anton's account and is not stated in the Eliade file or in any independent source reached.
stops.campa: Eliade suffers a stroke and is taken to the university hospital, where he lies eight days without recovering his speech. Culianu is at the bedside with Christinel Eliade and the household. He had been taught by this man by post, across an ocean, for three years before the two of them met. What he inherits is the library, an unfinished history of religious ideas, and a Bucharest of the 1930s that was never explained to anybody. Eliade dies on the twenty-second of April, at seventy-nine.
suggested_refs: The Mircea Eliade Papers, University of Chicago Library Special Collections
sources: Tereza Culianu-Petrescu, family chronology, in Antohi (ed.), Omul si opera

stops.name: Rockefeller Memorial Chapel, the reading
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to Culianu's part. The memorial service itself is attested and carries a stop in the atlas file for Eliade at these coordinates, which are inherited unchanged; that file names only Saul Bellow as reading. Culianu's co-reading comes from the family chronology and the memorial-service accounts characterised in the dossier and could not be independently confirmed. Day within May not recorded.
stops.campa: At the memorial in Rockefeller Chapel the readings are given by Saul Bellow and by Culianu. The university buries its dead in the grandest room it owns, Gothic and vaulted and cold in a Chicago spring. Culianu reads from Eliade in the accent both men carried out of Romania. The accounts of the service name Bellow; that Culianu read with him comes from the family. Within four years he will be printing, in Romanian, what Eliade wrote in the 1930s and never retracted.
suggested_refs: Rockefeller Memorial Chapel, 5850 South Woodlawn Avenue, Chicago
sources: Memorial-service accounts per the research dossier

stops.name: Chicago, Hillary Wiesner
stops.date_confidence: Engagement attested, circumstances reconstructed, one detail corrected. English Wikipedia confirms Hillary Wiesner as his fiancee at the time of his death and describes her then as a twenty-seven-year-old graduate student at Harvard University, not a Chicago Divinity School doctoral student as the geography pass had it. The University of Chicago finding aid, read in full, does not mention her at all, so it cannot corroborate anything here. The May 1986 meeting is dossier-only.
stops.campa: He meets Hillary Susan Wiesner, a graduate student at Harvard working on Arabic and comparative religion. He is thirty-six. They become collaborators first, then partners, then engaged, and over the next four years they travel together to Italy, France, Switzerland, Egypt and Israel. She is twenty-seven and they are engaged when he is shot. She keeps a diary through the years they are together, and one line from it was read aloud at a memorial for him a quarter of a century later.
stops.quote: He's a walking encyclopedia of religions and knows everything but the truth.

stops.campa: He takes a fellowship at the Netherlands Institute for Advanced Study at Wassenaar, in the dunes behind The Hague, to finish the French state doctorate: a comparative anatomy of the dualist movements of the West, from the Gnostics through the Bogomils to the Cathars. He has stopped asking who influenced whom. He is asking what a mind does when it is handed the premise that this world was badly made. The answer comes back the same in Alexandria, in Bulgaria and in Languedoc.

It is the third and highest of his doctorates, the one that in the French system certifies a man for a chair, and he takes it at thirty-seven with a post at last waiting for him across the Atlantic. The English version, The Tree of Gnosis, appears in 1992, a year after he is dead. Even the year of the defence is contested: the biographical record says January 1987, the thesis catalogue numbers it 1986.

stops.name: Groningen, the divorce
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The finalisation date of 30 January 1987 is from the family chronology; the surviving contemporary material on the marriage's end is partisan on both sides, notably Carmen Georgescu's 1986 letters to Christinel Eliade, and none of it is a judicial finding. English Wikipedia independently notes only that Culianu was divorced from his first wife by the time of his death.
stops.campa: The marriage to Carmen Georgescu ends. The divorce is finalised in the Netherlands at the end of January, in the same weeks he is defending in Paris and shifting his base to Chicago. What survives of it in the record is partisan on both sides: her letters to Christinel Eliade on one hand, his silence on the other, and no court's account of either. Andrei, the stepson, is grown. The Netherlands had given him his first documents, his first salary and eleven years of work. He does not live in Europe again.

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Old City
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the pin is a placeholder. stops.campa: He travels with Wiesner: Italy repeatedly, France, Switzerland, Egypt, Israel. In Jerusalem the comparatist walks the ground his books treat as structure, the same few hundred metres of stone that the ascent literature he catalogued in his Sorbonne thesis takes for the hinge of the world. Moshe Idel, his friend, is in these same years remaking the study of Kabbalah on a principle close to his own, that a mystical text is a technique and not a mood. No source reached names one site of the Israeli itinerary.

stops.name: 1700 East 56th Street, the burglary
stops.date_confidence: Address attested, burglary reconstructed. The FBI investigative file gives the address, 1700 East 56th Street, Apartment 906, Chicago; the file's text was searched specifically for a burglary or break-in and contains none, so the break-in, the items taken and the November 1989 date are all reconstruction from the biographical and investigative literature. Coordinates are the Nominatim geocode of 1700 East 56th Street, 41.7937 / -87.5832, correcting an earlier figure 500 m off. The affidavit quoted is from December 1989.
stops.campa: He circulates appeals in Hyde Park for his brother-in-law Dan Petrescu, the Iasi dissident under house arrest for publishing abroad. Soon afterward the apartment on East 56th Street is broken into and equipment, disks and wine are taken or destroyed. Culianu reads it as a message from Bucharest. His student Greg Spinner and the Chicago police read it as Hyde Park in November, and the police establish no political connection at all. In December he swears his immigration affidavit.
stops.quote: I will always remain a staunch anti-communist. My political activities opposing communism, since my exile, have outweighed exponentially any political connection I may have had with the Communist Party.
stops.quote_source: Ioan Culianu, sworn affidavit to the United States Immigration and Naturalization Service, December 1989, reproduced in the FBI investigative file

stops.campa: From the Divinity School he begins to write publicly, in Romanian and in English, about the Legionary years: about the Iron Guard, about which Romanian intellectuals of the 1930s wrote what and where, and about his own teacher's place in that record. The archive is in the same university library. The widow is in the same city.
stops.quote: the most secret, the most bombastic, the most mystical and bungling fascist organization of pre-War Europe

stops.campa: He holds a visiting chair at Siena and Arezzo in the spring, back on the Italian ground that took him in as a case number eighteen years earlier, this time with a title and a stipend. He is publishing at speed in three languages: the dualism book in French, an English reworking already under way, Out of This World, a novel, essays, and a journal he has founded called Incognita for a cognitive study of religion that nobody else is yet doing. stops.name: Chicago, Scoptophilia
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The column 'Scoptophilia' in the New York Romanian weekly Lumea libera romaneasca, and its attacks on the National Salvation Front and Ion Iliescu, come from the dossier's synthesis of his periodical output; the periodicals themselves were not refetched, and no month is recorded. The quotation is verbatim from Eco's essay, but the chain is Culianu to Ted Anton's book to Eco, not Eco as eyewitness: Eco writes that Anton quotes a statement made by Culianu during the discussion of Eco's book in New York.
stops.campa: He writes for Lumea libera romaneasca, the Romanian weekly out of New York, and runs a column called Scoptophilia against the National Salvation Front and against Ion Iliescu. The thesis is blunt and he repeats it everywhere: December 1989 was not a revolution but a coup, staged by the apparatus that had run the country, and the apparatus is running it still. He had put the general mechanism to Umberto Eco a year earlier in New York, talking about the plots occultists invent and then move into.
stops.quote: Nothing reveals this principle more than the Holocaust.... When crazed minds are in synchrony they create an alternative reality; they kill for invented reasons.
stops.quote_source: Culianu at a New York discussion of Umberto Eco's novel, reported by Ted Anton and quoted by Eco, 'Murder in Chicago', New York Review of Books, 10 April 1997

stops.name: Chicago, the interview in 22
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the sense that the FBI investigative file records investigators' attention to the interview; the interview text itself was not refetched, and the 5 April 1991 date comes from the dossier's citation of that file. The substance is consistent with his documented pattern of exile-press polemic. The quotation is his own from the December 1989 immigration affidavit and is dated there, not here.
stops.campa: He gives an interview to the Bucharest magazine 22, saying inside the country and over his own name what he has been printing in the exile press: that the revolution was a coup, that the Securitate networks were never dismantled, that the men now governing are the men who were governing before. Copies circulate in Bucharest and in Chicago. The interview will be among the first documents the federal investigators pull. He has not set foot in Romania for nineteen years.
stops.quote: I have been constantly engaged in activities meant to expose the crimes and the failure of the Communist dictatorship in Romania.
stops.quote_source: Ioan Culianu, sworn affidavit to the United States Immigration and Naturalization Service, December 1989, reproduced in the FBI investigative file

stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the threat is uncorroborated. stops.campa: Former King Michael I comes to Chicago, and Culianu, who has opposed restoration in print, meets him and comes away thinking a monarch might steady a constitution that nobody else is steadying. He takes a public part in the events at the Drake Hotel. The family will say afterward that a man approached him in the hotel and told him he would be killed if he worked with the king. That threat is reported only after the murder, and it is in none of the police records reviewed in the case.

stops.name: Swift Hall, the stall on the third floor
stops.date_confidence: Attested, from the FBI investigative file read directly, with one internal contradiction left standing. The file names the stall inconsistently, once as the fourth and once as 'stall number five, closest to the window', where the fired bullet and the Winchester .25 automatic spent cartridge were found; the stronger verbatim reading is used here and the inconsistency is in the source, not resolved. The file gives both 1:05 and 1:15 p.m.; English Wikipedia says 'at noon'. Coordinates as corrected for Swift Hall.
stops.campa: At about one o'clock he goes into the third-floor men's room and sits down in a stall. Someone in the next stall shoots him once through the back of the head with a .25 calibre automatic. The door is locked from the inside; he is found there. On the floor beside the toilet in the stall closest to the window lie a fired bullet and a Winchester .25 Auto cartridge case. His wallet is in his pocket and his money is in his wallet. No weapon is recovered, then or since.

The Cook County medical examiner records a gunshot homicide. Nobody in the building heard the shot through the tiled wall. Wiesner is in another city and has to be reached by telephone. The Chicago police and the Federal Bureau of Investigation open files that week. The case is still open.

stops.name: Swift Hall, no plaque
stops.date_confidence: Attested as testimony, dated to the observation. Sorin Antohi's account in the memorial volume he edited is explicitly dated April 1992 and is quoted below verbatim from the archive.org text of that volume; the volume's own publication year is not stated in the text fetched. The Romanian sales figure of several hundred thousand copies is Antohi's own, in the same volume, and is not independently confirmed. Day is an ordering default.
stops.campa: Less than a year after the murder Sorin Antohi passes through the Divinity School and finds nothing: no plaque, no notice, no talk of one, and the dead professor's presence in the building carefully removed. In Romania the opposite is happening at speed. His sister and Dan Petrescu bring the books out as fast as they can be set, and Culianu, unpublishable in his own country for the nineteen years he was alive in exile, sells there in the hundreds of thousands.
stops.quote: no talk whatsoever of institutionalizing the memory of the talented Professor Culianu, at least through a memorial plaque

stops.campa: His papers come to the university's Special Collections, into the reading room that holds Eliade's: notes, drafts, the unfinished cognitive project, the nineteen years of letters with the man whose field he inherited and whose past he went into the archive after. At the twenty-fifth anniversary his former student Gregory Spinner spoke at the memorial.
